details:
**Neil Bartlett and xenon hexafluoroplatinate**
In 1962 Neil Bartlett made the first noble gas compound by reacting xenon with platinum hexafluoride, producing an orange-yellow solid. He tried the reaction because platinum hexafluoride had already oxidized molecular oxygen, and O2 has a first ionization energy close to xenon's. The result overturned the belief that noble gases could not form compounds.

**Full valence shells and inertness**
Noble gases make up Group 18 (also called Group 8A or Group 0), the far-right column of the periodic table. Their outer shells are completely filled: eight valence electrons satisfy the octet rule, except helium, which has two. This makes them monatomic and very unreactive, which is why they are also called inert gases.

**Brackets in shorthand electron configurations**
In abbreviated (noble gas) electron configurations, the symbol of the preceding noble gas is written in square brackets to stand for the filled inner shells, followed by the remaining valence electrons, as in [Ne]3s1 for sodium.

**Highest ionization energies and smallest radii**
Because their effective nuclear charge is high, noble gases have the highest first ionization energy and the smallest atomic radius in each period. Helium has the highest first ionization energy of any element and the smallest atomic radius.

**Xenon fluorides (XeF2, XeF4, XeF6)**
Xenon reacts with fluorine to form stable compounds that break the octet rule: linear xenon difluoride, square planar xenon tetrafluoride, and xenon hexafluoride. These are among the best-known noble gas compounds.

**Excimer lasers**
Excimer ("excited dimer") lasers use molecules that exist only in an excited state. The first excimer laser used a xenon dimer, and most now combine a noble gas with a halogen, such as xenon chloride, which emits ultraviolet light at 308 nanometers.

**London dispersion forces and the Lennard-Jones potential**
Noble gas atoms interact only through weak, isotropic van der Waals forces, mainly London dispersion forces, which gives them very low melting and boiling points. The Lennard-Jones potential models these interactions especially well, and it was fitted in part to data on argon.

**Argon and potassium-argon dating**
Potassium-40 decays into argon-40 (by electron capture), so the ratio of the two dates volcanic rocks. A refined version, argon-argon dating, compares argon-40 with argon-39. Argon makes up about 1 percent of Earth's atmosphere, making it the third most abundant gas there, and it is commonly used as the fill gas in Geiger counters.

**Helium and the alpha particle**
The alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus. Helium was first detected as an unexpected line in the Sun's spectrum, is the second most abundant element in the universe, and is lighter than air, so it fills balloons. It has the lowest melting and boiling points of any element.

**Superfluid helium (lambda point and Rollin film)**
Below the lambda point, liquid helium-4 becomes a superfluid with zero viscosity. The lambda point is named for the shape of the heat capacity versus temperature curve. Superfluid helium creeps up container walls as a thin Rollin film and shows the fountain effect. David Lee, Douglas Osheroff, and Robert Richardson discovered superfluidity in helium-3, where the fermionic atoms form Cooper pairs, and dilution refrigerators reach very low temperatures by mixing helium-3 and helium-4.

**Radon in basements**
Radon is a radioactive noble gas produced by uranium decay in rock and soil. It builds up in basements, and indoor radon is a leading cause of lung cancer. It is measured with Lucas cells, and the Watras incident of 1984, when engineer Stanley Watras set off radiation alarms at a nuclear plant from radon in his home, drew public attention to the problem.

**Oganesson**
The heaviest noble gas, element 118, formerly called ununoctium. It was made by bombarding californium with calcium ions and named after Yuri Oganessian. Along with seaborgium, it is one of only two elements named after a person who was alive at the time.

**Xenon anesthetic and flashlamps**
Xenon is a more potent, though much more expensive, general anesthetic than nitrous oxide. It is also the main gas in flashlamps. Xenon-129 in meteorites comes from the decay of the extinct isotope iodine-129.

**Trimix and heliox breathing gases**
Deep-sea divers breathe mixtures in which helium replaces some or all of the nitrogen, such as heliox (helium and oxygen) and trimix (oxygen, nitrogen, and helium). This reduces nitrogen narcosis and the risk of decompression sickness at great depths.

**William Ramsay and fractional distillation of liquid air**
William Ramsay won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering the noble gases. In 1898 he and Morris Travers isolated neon, krypton, and xenon by fractional distillation of liquid air, after he and Lord Rayleigh had discovered argon in 1894.
